newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel defends settlements, PLO urges confrontation.
newsitem.headline: Israel defends settlements, PLO urges confrontation.

text.p: Israel on Saturday defended its decision to grant financial benefits to Jewish settlers in the West Bank as the PLO urged Palestinians to confront Jewish settlement by "all possible means".

"The government stands behind its policies to aid the settlers who stand bravely every day against waves of terror," Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's spokesman Shai Bazak said in a statement.

In self-ruled Gaza late on Friday, Palestinian President Yasser Arafat's cabinet blasted an Israeli government decision reached hours earlier to provide financial benefits to Jewish settlers in the occupied West Bank.
"Israel's measures aim at destroying the peace process and leading the whole region to the edge of an explosion," said a statement released after the Palestinian cabinet meeting.

The incentives, which could entice more Jews to settle in the area Israel occupied in the 1967 Middle East War, were seen as a strong sign of defiance by the right-wing Netanyahu to world opposition to his plans to tighten Israel's hold on captured Arab land.
"The Palestinian leadership calls on the masses everywhere to firmly confront with all possible means the Israeli settlement aggression in order to defend the land."

Netanyahu's cabinet on Friday decided to reinstate benefits for West Bank settlers, such as lower taxes, that are already given to residents of disadvantaged towns inside Israel, and to Israelis in the occupied Gaza Strip and Golan Heights.
The move came two days after radical Palestinian gunmen killed a settler and her 12-year-old son in a drive-by shooting near PLO-ruled Ramallah in the West Bank.
European Union leaders at a summit in Dublin on Saturday voiced grave concern over deteriorating Middle East peace moves and roundly condemned Jewish settlement in occupied lands.
"The settlements issue is eroding confidence in the peace process," a European statement said. "Settlements contravene international law and are a major obstacle to peace."

Israel's main ally Washington, going beyond standard U.S. phraseology, called the settlement incentive decision "troubling", suggesting it could hamper peace talks as a step "seen to pre-empt the outcome of a negotiation."

The fate of settlements, in which more than 130,000 Jews live among the two million Arabs of the West Bank and Gaza, is to be decided in final status peace talks that have yet to resume under Netanyahu.

Since taking office in June, the Netanyahu government has given the go-ahead for the construction of thousands of homes in existing settlements but has yet to meet the demands of settler leaders to establish new outposts.

He also has yet to make good on a pledge by Israel's previous centre-left government to withdraw its troops from parts of the West Bank town of Hebron. Palestinians see implementation of the signed deal as a litmus test of Netanyahu's intentions on peace.
